Historical observations for this pairing reflect a combination of sources. The earlier part of the record is based on measurements of gases trapped in the layers of ice covering Antarctica. More recent measurements come from air monitoring stations at several locations around the world, starting with carbon dioxide measurements that have been collected continually at Mauna Loa, Hawaii, since 1959. The three gases measured (carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrous oxide) are relatively long-lived and globally mixed, so concentrations measured anywhere on Earth can generally represent the global average. Still, some variation can be seen in the graphs, particularly for methane, which has the shortest atmospheric lifetime among these three gases. 

Model outputs shown here are the official concentration data sets associated with each of the major emissions scenarios. These concentrations were inputs that were used in running each of the global climate models whose results are reported in the project team’s other observation/projection pairings.
